newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronaut seeks to cast vote from space.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronaut seeks to cast vote from space.

text.p: U.S. astronaut John Blaha said on Thursday he hoped the fact he was sailing through space 250 miles (402 km) above the nearest polling station would not stop him from voting in the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential election.
Blaha, on a four-month mission aboard Russia's Mir space station, said he would be unable to cast his vote in person and asked whether his wife could vote for him.

After training in Russia for six months before his mission began, Blaha blasted off aboard the space shuttle Atlantis on Sept. 16, one week before absentee ballots were mailed out in Texas, NASA officials said.

"What I've always said is, if somebody would let my wife vote for me and I give her the authority to do that, that's how I could get my vote in," he said in a news conference televised from the space station.

The Texas secretary of state has no authority to allow Blaha to vote by proxy, so election officials have asked Gov. George Bush for a proclamation allowing him to vote from space, county elections officials said.

Tony Sirvello, administrator of elections in Harris County, which encompasses Houston and the Johnson Space Centre, also approached the Pentagon to determine whether Blaha could cast a ballot under a system set up for U.S. citizens and military personnel stationed overseas.
"I guess Mr. Blaha is as overseas as you can get," said Sirvello, who has been working since early September to find a way to allow Blaha, a registered voter in the county, to cast a ballot.

Blaha, a 54-year old veteran of four shuttle missions, said he did not vote for President Bill Clinton in the 1992 elections, but believes both Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole would do "a great job."

Blaha replaced astronaut Shannon Lucid on the Russian space station following her record-setting 188-day mission. He said he has been able to follow the baseball World Series with reports from ham radio operators and box scores of the games sent up by a space agency publicist.
